coverage.notes: Coverage is high for the two labs and for report format, and thin for homework: the sets reach across several heat-transfer topics whose instructor problem statements have not been read into this pack, so it states no solution method for any of them (see not_covered). No graded copy, instructor annotation or syllabus was found in either of the student's two document archives, searched by filename and, for every word-processor file, by checking for tracked changes and reviewer comments; none carries any. A syllabus did exist, since the lab schedule refers the student to it, but no copy is held. So every 'what good looks like' entry is derived from the professor's written handouts and lab manuals rather than from a marked-up submission. The student submissions backing them are reported by their author to have scored highly, which is the strongest evidence available here and is weaker than a graded artifact; they also break several written rules (page limits, title-page numbering), and the handout wins where they disagree. Homework format: two homework files were read as page images in September 2026 and show the student's layout, which the homework family records as observed practice rather than a requirement; the other sets have not been read that way, and no homework page carries a grader mark, a score or feedback. Margin size has no evidence at all.

evidence_tiers.spec: Professor-authored documents distributed in this course and term: general technical-report guidelines, the lab schedule with per-stage deliverable descriptions and grading, and both lab manuals.
evidence_tiers.prior_handout: A one-page writing-guidelines handout by the same professor, originally issued for an earlier ENGR 319 lab and filed with this course's lab material. Probably still applies, but it was not re-issued under this course's header.
evidence_tiers.exemplar: Observed in the student's own submissions. The author reports that this course's memos and lab reports scored highly, so the observed structure is reported to have worked; no graded copy or instructor annotation survives to confirm it, and the written handout still wins wherever the two disagree.
evidence_tiers.default: No evidence. A renderer default so the pipeline can run. Do not present it to the student as a course rule.
evidence_tiers.verification_note: The spec-tier documents were re-read directly and checked against this pack's format rules, rather than trusted from an earlier round's summary. Every rule checked held: unnumbered title page with a descriptive title, abstract on the title page carrying real numbers, headings that stand out, figure captions below stating the takeaway, no chart title on a captioned graph and never a 'Quantity A vs Quantity B' title, grayscale readability, no screen captures as figures, centred figures without text wrap, table captions above and allowed to be brief, schematic rather than photographic diagrams, units on every number including in appendices and on graph axes, equations set in the word processor's equation editor and woven into the text, 11 to 12 point classic fonts, 1.5 line spacing, stapled and collected at the start of class, and page numbers away from the stapling corner with the body starting at page 1. The per-stage page budget was confirmed independently: the schedule asks for 2 to 3 pages of written explanation per pre-submission, matching the maximum this pack encodes. The prior_handout tier was also confirmed rather than assumed: that handout is headed as writing guidelines for the earlier course and carries the same professor's name, which is what this pack already said about it. No contradiction was found between the documents and this pack.

methods.title: Moist-air state from dry- and wet-bulb temperatures
methods.when: Any A/C lab station (A, B, C, D), or a psychrometrics homework problem.
steps: Fix the state with three properties: measured atmospheric pressure, dry-bulb, and wet-bulb.
Use the moist-air property functions (per kg of dry air) with pressure passed explicitly; do not rely on a chart's built-in pressure.
Read humidity ratio, enthalpy per kg dry air, and specific volume at every station.
Water-vapour flow at a station is the dry-air mass flow times the humidity ratio.
pitfalls: Using a refrigerant gauge pressure (or any refrigerant pressure) as the moist-air pressure.
Treating the inlet air as dry; ambient air already carries water vapour.
Dropping measured atmospheric pressure in favour of a standard atmosphere.
methods.basis: The A/C laboratory manual, read directly: it defines the station states and the measured inputs they are fixed from. Passing total pressure explicitly on every moist-air call is a tool-level rule from the shared EES pack, reinforced here because one early version of the student's own model passed a refrigerant-loop pressure instead.

methods.title: Dry-air mass flow from the orifice-plate manometer
methods.when: A/C lab; needed before any per-section balance.
steps: Take the manometer pressure drop and the moist-air specific volume at the exit station.
Apply the manual's orifice correlation, attaching units to its constant so the equation solver checks dimensions.
Use this one dry-air flow for every section, since dry air is conserved along the duct.
pitfalls: Using the specific volume at the wrong station.
Leaving the correlation constant unitless, which hides unit errors.
methods.basis: The A/C laboratory manual, which gives the orifice relation and the manometer reading it takes. Using the specific volume at the exit station is the manual's own choice, not an inference. The Pa-versus-kPa trap inside the square root is observed in the student's working files and is recorded as a check.

methods.title: Forcing versus response mass and energy accounting
methods.when: The core of every A/C section analysis (A-B, B-C, C-D), for both water and energy, in both seasons.
steps: Draw the control volume for the section around the air stream and list every term that crosses it.

Compute each forcing term independently from its own measurement: electrical heaters from supply voltage squared over resistance, summed in parallel (never nameplate kW); fan power from the manual's voltage-to-power chart; steam or condensate mass and the enthalpy it carries; refrigerant heat absorption.
Compute the response term independently from the air-stream states: dry-air flow times the change in humidity ratio (water) or the change in enthalpy (energy).
Report percent error as (response minus forcing) over forcing.
Where no forcing is applied, normalise the response difference by the inlet value instead, since forcing-based error is undefined.
Keep one sign convention throughout: into the air stream is positive, out of it is negative.
pitfalls: Solving the balance for an unknown the way a homework problem would. A 0% error means the forcing term was derived from the response, which defeats the experiment.
Omitting enthalpy carried by mass streams (steam in, condensate out).
Leaving fan power out of the energy forcing.
Refrigerant heat is energy leaving the air; sign it accordingly.
In section A-B, summer: two control-volume formulations are required and must be compared, giving six error findings in that stage instead of four.
methods.basis: The A/C laboratory manual, which is where the whole forcing-versus-response idea comes from, together with the lab schedule's per-stage descriptions of what each submission must account for. The manual supplies the percent-error definition and the sign convention. The rule that a zero percent error is a red flag, meaning the balance was solved for the forcing term, is this pack's reading of what the manual is asking for rather than a sentence the manual contains.

methods.title: Steam generation rate from a boiler energy balance
methods.when: A/C lab section A-B, summer (steam generator on).
steps: Put a control volume around the steam generator at steady state: tap water in equals steam out.
Net heat equals the electrical heater power minus the convective loss to the room (the manual's hA constant times the temperature difference).
Steam mass rate is net heat over the enthalpy rise from tap-water state to saturated vapour at room pressure.
This mass rate is the water forcing term for A-B.
pitfalls: Using the saturated-liquid state (quality 0) for tap water; tap water enters subcooled at room temperature.
Assuming a boiling temperature instead of evaluating saturation at the measured room pressure.
methods.basis: The A/C laboratory manual, which gives the steam-generator sub-model, its electrical input and its convective loss. That tap water is subcooled and not quality zero is the manual's own framing; it is repeated here because treating it as saturated liquid is the obvious slip.

methods.title: R134a vapour-compression cycle from measured gauge data
methods.when: A/C lab: evaporator heat for section B-C, and the system-level COP and compressor isentropic efficiency in the final report.
steps: Convert every refrigerant gauge pressure to absolute pressure before any property lookup.
Fix states 1-3 from the measured temperature and pressure.
Fix state 4 (evaporator inlet), which is not measured: assume saturated liquid at the condenser outlet and an isenthalpic expansion valve, so h4 = h3.
Evaporator heat is refrigerant mass flow times (h1 minus h4); compressor work is mass flow times (h2 minus h1).
COP is evaporator heat over compressor work. Compressor isentropic efficiency compares the isentropic enthalpy rise (outlet at state-1 entropy and state-2 pressure) with the actual rise.
Plot the four states on a P-h diagram for each season.
pitfalls: Using gauge pressure directly in a property call.
Reading the float flow meter anywhere but its lowest steady value at the top edge of the float, as the manual directs.
Putting condensate on the condenser side; air-side condensate forms at the evaporator.
methods.basis: The A/C laboratory manual for the refrigerant loop, its measured gauge pressures and the states it asks for. The two assumptions that close the cycle, saturated liquid at the condenser outlet and an isenthalpic valve, are the manual's. Converting gauge to absolute before any property call is a check this pack adds, from a failure mode rather than from the manual.

methods.title: Evaporator effectiveness and UA (extra credit)
steps: Treat the evaporating refrigerant as the infinite-capacity stream, so the capacity ratio is zero.
Effectiveness is actual heat transfer over maximum possible heat transfer.
Use the effectiveness-NTU relation at zero capacity ratio to get NTU, then UA.
pitfalls: Assigning a finite refrigerant heat capacity during phase change.
methods.basis: The A/C laboratory manual and the lab schedule, which mark this as extra credit rather than required. The capacity-ratio-zero simplification follows from the manual's own description of the evaporator; the effectiveness-NTU treatment itself is standard and is not written out in any instructor document in the archive.

methods.title: Actual combustion equation with unburned fuel
methods.when: IC lab energy analysis. Precedes every exhaust calculation.
steps: Solve the theoretical (100% air) octane balance element by element in the equation solver; do not look it up.
Code the O2 and N2 molar fractions of air as editable parameters and compute the N:O ratio from them rather than hard-coding it.
Compute the actual molar air-fuel ratio from the measured air and fuel mass flows and their molar masses.
Solve the six-unknown actual equation (n, a, b, c, d, e) from four element balances, the burned-fuel oxygen relation, and the measured air-fuel ratio. Keep the manual's letters.
Confirm that either unburned fuel (a) or excess O2 (d) is zero, never both nonzero.
pitfalls: Writing species symbols into the balances; code only the coefficient equations and comment each one.
Not sanity-checking the actual air-fuel ratio against the manual's expected band; being well below theoretical is normal for this engine.
methods.basis: The IC engine laboratory manual, read directly, which supplies the coefficient letters this method uses, the expected band for the actual air-fuel ratio, and the instruction to solve the theoretical balance element by element. That exactly one of unburned fuel or excess oxygen is nonzero is the manual's framing. A homework prompt STATES the same approach a second time: let the solver balance the coefficients element by element, as practice for this lab, and never write the overall reaction as a solver equation. Keeping the oxygen and nitrogen fractions as an editable parameter rather than hard-coding the ratio is observed in the student's lab model and in a worked homework page. The balance also rests, for two problems, on the student's own worked homework pages, whose final value matches the answer the prompt itself lists: the reaction balanced species by species with each coefficient tracked by element, the air-fuel ratio from the balanced moles and molecular masses, and the same element balances written as solver equations. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded.

methods.title: IC intake-air and exhaust mass flow
steps: Intake air mass flow from the Bernoulli orifice relation with the manual's discharge coefficient and orifice diameter; use the magnitude of the pressure drop.
Fuel mass flow from timed pipette volume times liquid n-octane density.
Exhaust mass flow is intake air plus fuel.
pitfalls: Mixing Pa and kPa inside the square root; convert explicitly before the root.
Carrying a negative gauge reading into the square root.
Mislabeling ambient-pressure units, which silently corrupts every downstream property.
methods.basis: The IC engine laboratory manual, which gives the orifice relation, the timed-pipette fuel measurement, and exhaust flow as air plus fuel. Using the magnitude of the pressure drop, and the unit trap inside the square root, are checks recorded from observed failure modes.

methods.title: Exhaust specific heat: mixture prediction vs calorimeter
methods.when: IC lab energy analysis, before finalising the energy balance.
steps: Predict mixture cp from the product mole fractions and each species' cp, converted consistently between molar and mass bases.
From the counter-flow calorimeter, set water heat gain equal to exhaust heat loss using the four measured temperatures and both mass flows, and solve for experimental exhaust cp.
Compare the two and discuss the gap.
pitfalls: Evaluating a species in the wrong phase.
Ignoring water-vapour condensation in the calorimeter when explaining a large gap.
methods.basis: The IC engine laboratory manual, which describes the calorimeter and asks for the predicted mixture specific heat to be compared against the experimental value. The comparison is the manual's requirement; how close the two should land is not stated anywhere in the archive and is not asserted here.

methods.title: Engine steady-state energy balance
methods.when: IC lab energy analysis, at the energy-data operating point.
steps: Air intake energy: split air into O2 and N2 and use ideal-gas enthalpies, which include formation enthalpy.
Fuel energy: liquid octane formation enthalpy from the textbook table, adjusted from 25 °C to the inlet temperature (taken as ambient).
Exhaust energy: exhaust mass flow times mixture enthalpy at cylinder exhaust temperature, averaged over the five product species on a consistent basis.
Shaft power is torque times angular speed, in SI.
Heat loss to the room is the residual of in = out. Spark-plug power is neglected.
Present the drop in chemical energy (reactants minus products) and show that it equals shaft power plus heat loss.
pitfalls: Using the generic 'air' substance or humid-air functions in the combustion balance; the reference state differs.
Calling a formation-enthalpy function on real liquids.
Panicking at negative absolute energies; only differences matter.
Torque units that a case-insensitive solver reads as nanometres.
methods.basis: The IC engine laboratory manual for the streams and the order they are built in, and the lab schedule, which flags this as the longest analysis and tells students to work well ahead. Two substantive rules are the manual's own: air energy uses the oxygen and nitrogen ideal-gas enthalpies rather than a generic air substance, and liquid-octane formation enthalpy comes from the textbook table adjusted to inlet temperature. That heat loss is the residual, and that negative absolute enthalpies are expected and harmless, are the manual's framing. A homework prompt STATES the formation-enthalpy rules a second time: an ideal-gas enthalpy lookup already includes formation, while a liquid fuel needs its formation enthalpy supplied from the textbook. For two problems the student's own worked homework pages, whose final value matches the answer the prompt itself lists, show an enthalpy of combustion assembled from the formation enthalpies of reactants and products, and an adiabatic energy balance built from ideal-gas product enthalpies and a textbook liquid-fuel formation enthalpy. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded.

methods.title: Engine power and torque curves
steps: At each of the several engine speeds, shaft power is torque times angular speed.
Plot power and torque against speed on one figure with two labelled axes.
State the peak power and peak torque, each with the speed where it occurs.
pitfalls: Assuming peak torque and peak power share a speed.
Adding a chart title on top of the caption.
methods.basis: The IC engine laboratory manual and the lab schedule's description of this pre-submission. That peak power and peak torque need not occur at the same speed is the manual's point, and it is the finding the stage asks for. Excel being acceptable for this plot is stated in the schedule's stage description.

methods.title: Overall thermal efficiency vs engine power
methods.when: IC lab efficiency pre-submission and final.
steps: Overall thermal efficiency is shaft power over (lower heating value times fuel mass flow).
Compute it at every operating speed.
Plot efficiency against shaft power, ordering points by power rather than by run number, and discuss how efficiency changes with load.
pitfalls: Using the higher heating value.
Plotting against speed when the required plot is against power.
methods.basis: The IC engine laboratory manual and the lab schedule. Plotting efficiency against engine power rather than against speed or run number is the stage's stated requirement, and it is the one thing that distinguishes this analysis from the power-curve stage.

methods.title: Assembling the final report from pre-submissions
steps: Correct earlier sections with feedback and later understanding before assembling.
Condense three pre-submissions into the final's body budget; each section keeps a brief result and conclusion that points to its appendix.

Add the system-level results the pre-submissions did not require (A/C: P-h and psychrometric charts, COP, compressor isentropic efficiency, optional effectiveness; IC: overall conclusions on energies and efficiencies).
Move detail to lettered appendices and decide whether repeated material stays or is merged.
Close with per-section conclusions, then overall conclusions on error magnitude, plausibility, error sources, and how to reduce them.
pitfalls: Stapling the three pre-submissions together.
Blowing the body page limit; both final-report exemplars in the archive ran long, which is not a pattern to copy.
methods.basis: The lab schedule, overwhelmingly: it is the document that defines the pre-submission-to-final rhythm, the due order, the per-stage page budgets and what each stage must contain. The observation that the final is a rewrite to a tighter budget rather than the pre-submissions stapled together is drawn from comparing the student's own pre-submissions against the final, and is exemplar-tier.

methods.title: Homework solved in EES
methods.when: Homework problems the set marks for EES.
steps: Header comment block with course, assignment, and problem number, and the student name as [Student Name].
Givens with units attached, then the solution blocks in the order of the problem parts.
Print the code, with the requested answers visible as key variables in the solution output.
Check against any answer the prompt supplies, and mark the answer where the prompt asks for it to be marked.
pitfalls: Submitting problems out of the assigned order.
Using EES on a set that says it is not an EES set.
methods.basis: The per-set header instructions on the weekly homework sheets, read for all eleven available sets: submit in the assigned order, print solver code for the problems that set names with solutions as key variables, and a collaboration rule. Two prompts read in full STATE more: outputs printed in order as key variables with descriptive labels and correct units; a single answer may be circled or highlighted in the solver output; and a spreadsheet printout, where a set assigns one, made professional with units and labels. The layout also rests, for two problems, on the student's own printed solver solutions, whose final value matches the answer the prompt itself lists: a header comment block, the givens with units, a comment naming the source table of each tabulated constant, one block per part or regime, and the requested answers as key variables. A student page counts here only where its final value matches the prompt's listed answer, and no value from any page is recorded. How a homework solution done by hand should be laid out is not established by any instructor document; the observed practice for it is recorded on the homework family as practice, not as the course's method.

stage_delta: Every pre-submission is a self-contained short report (title page with abstract, Objective, Methods, Results, Conclusions, Appendix) covering both seasons for one duct section; the written pages must tell the whole story if the attachments were lost.

The EES model is one file per season, and it grows each stage: stage one holds the givens, station states, and dry-air flow plus the C-D balance; each later stage appends a section block and corrects earlier blocks; the final adds the cycle metrics. The observed file grew several-fold between the first submission and the final.
Corrections are expected between stages; the final is not the sum of the pre-submissions but a rewrite to a tighter budget.
System-level cycle results (COP, isentropic efficiency, P-h and psychrometric charts) are required only at the final, though including charts earlier is harmless.

what_good_looks_like: Forcing and response are computed independently, and every error is nonzero and explained in physical terms (single-point wet-bulb sampling across a non-uniform duct is the expected dominant source).
Each section's table sets forcing, response, and percent error side by side for both seasons, with units in the headings and sensible significant digits.
The control-volume figure shows exactly the terms used in that section's balance and nothing else.
The abstract states the error range and cycle metrics as numbers with units.
No-forcing cases use the inlet-normalised error rather than dividing by zero.
The final fits the body budget and every chart has a takeaway caption, no chart title, and is legible in grayscale.
assignment_families.basis: The A/C laboratory manual and the lab schedule, both instructor-written and read directly, for the apparatus, the stage order, the per-stage deliverables and the page budgets. The student's submissions for this lab are exemplar-tier and show shape only; where they and the handouts disagree, the handouts win.

what_good_looks_like: The actual air-fuel ratio is computed from measured flows, sits inside the manual's expected band, and drives the combustion coefficients.
Exactly one of unburned fuel or excess oxygen is nonzero, and the report says which and why.
Predicted and calorimeter exhaust cp are compared and the gap is explained.
The energy table shows the chemical-energy drop equal to shaft power plus heat loss, with the heat loss identified as a residual.
The power curves state both peaks with their speeds, and the report notes whether they coincide.
Efficiency is plotted against power (not speed or run number) and its trend with load is discussed.

The student's submissions are exemplar-tier and show shape only; where they and the handouts disagree, the handouts win.

assignment_families.title: Weekly homework sets

assistance_rules.summary: The sets state that homework may be worked on together but that code must not be shared.
assistance_rules.applies_to: Any request to write, complete or repair EES code for a homework problem in this course.
assistance_rules.not_generalised: It is not clear how this applies to code a tool writes for the student, as opposed to code another student wrote. The rule predates the question and does not answer it. It is not resolved in either direction here.
required_behaviour: Surface the rule to the student once, before helping with an EES homework problem, and say plainly that whether it covers tool-written code is a judgement for them and their professor, not for this tool.
Then follow their decision. Do not repeat it on every request.
Do not refuse on the strength of an ambiguity the course has not settled; inventing a prohibition substitutes this tool's judgement for the professor's.
assistance_rules.basis: The homework sets for the observed term, read directly. Stated on several of the later sets, not on every set, so it is treated as the course's standing rule rather than as specific to those weeks. The unresolved question about tool-written code is this pack's observation, not something the course says.

must_contain: printed EES code with key answers visible, for the specific problems that set names; which problems require EES is stated per set and is not a blanket rule
for a problem solved in more than one tool, each solve printed and the results compared rather than one silently replacing the other
a spreadsheet printout, professional with units and labels, for a problem the set assigns to a spreadsheet
stage_details.tool_note: Hand work is common for problems the set does not assign to EES, and the archive shows those written directly on the printed prompt. It is not the only alternative to EES, so do not treat the choice as EES-or-hand. The archive also shows a spreadsheet used to tabulate and plot results a solver produced, and a CAD thermal simulation used to re-solve a conduction problem that had already been solved numerically. At least one set assigns a problem to a spreadsheet in its own words, so a spreadsheet can be the assigned tool and not only the student's choice. Follow whatever the set assigns; where it assigns nothing, the tool is the student's choice.
stage_details.evidence_note: The per-set header instructions, and the full text of two prompts, are the written spec. Completed non-EES work has no text layer; two sets were read as page images and show the student's own ink, with no instructor feedback on any page. The multi-tool pattern is observed in the student's own files, not stated in any instructor document. One of those files is a simulation of a part that a numerical solve elsewhere in the archive also covers, but it is a steady-state run filed with the following week's set and dated between the two, so which set it was submitted with is ambiguous.

deliverables: problem solutions in assigned order; EES printouts for EES problems
what_good_looks_like: Each EES problem prints its givens with units, its solution blocks in problem-part order, and the requested answers as key variables.
Where the prompt supplies an answer, the solution reproduces it or explains the difference.

rules: A set may assign a problem to a spreadsheet. The printed table is then made professional, with units and labels.
Solver outputs are printed in order as key variables, with descriptive labels and correct units. Where a problem has a single answer, it may be circled or highlighted in the solver output.
Comparison problems ask for a written comment on the comparison, and for like-for-like quantities and units before comparing.

Some prompts direct which solver facilities to use: one asks that reaction coefficients be balanced element by element in the solver rather than written as one overall equation, and another asks that a built-in solver function not be relied on because it does not help learning.
The solver is not available on tests, and one prompt says so while asking for solver work, so that property lookups by hand are worth practising alongside it.
stated_presentation.basis: the typed text of two homework prompts, read directly; these are the instructor's own words, not an inference from the worked pages

observed_practice.status: OBSERVED STUDENT PRACTICE in two archived homework files, not an instructor requirement. The instructor's stated rules are in stated_presentation and in the weekly set's must_contain.
observed_practice.medium: Hand work in digital ink, written below the problem's own text on the prompt page. Problems a set assigns to the solver or to a spreadsheet appear as their printed output.
observed_practice.layout: For combustion, the reaction is written out with each coefficient boxed and colour-coded by element as it is balanced. The relation is written before the numbers, and the final value is boxed with its unit.
observed_practice.method: Solver printouts open with a header comment block, list the givens with units, name in a comment the table each tabulated constant came from, run one block per part or regime, and end with the requested answers as key variables. The spreadsheet printout carries a header block and colour-codes its formation-enthalpy and sensible-enthalpy columns.
observed_practice.assembly: Each homework is one PDF assembled by the student: the prompt pages, the worked pages, and the solver and spreadsheet printouts, in problem order.
observed_practice.basis: two homework files, 20 pages, read as page images in September 2026; the text layer carries only the typed prompt and the printouts, so the ink is invisible to text extraction; the other homework sets have not been read this way

unknown: whether the instructor requires any of the observed layout, or would accept a different one
what the grader accepted: no page carries a grader mark, a score or feedback

textbook_references.book_note: The labels below were collected from the student's own working files, and none of those files names the textbook by title or edition. The course document set has since been searched too, and no instructor handout names it either; the identification exists but comes from outside this pack and is recorded with the shared textbook records rather than here. This course pair uses more than one book, a thermodynamics text and a heat-transfer text, which is exactly why a bare label is unsafe: the same label denotes different tables in different books. Never resolve one of these labels against a book the student has not confirmed, and never cite a value read from one.
textbook_references.migration_status: These are plain text and promise nothing. A shared textbook index exists for this book's appendix only; in-chapter tables and figures, which is what every label below is, are not indexed yet. Until that lands these citations cannot be resolved mechanically, and this note should not be read as saying they will be.

attestation.claim: Typically 1-2% deducted per report, 5% at worst; roughly 95-99%.
attestation.note: Self-reported, recalled rather than read off a returned copy. Raises what the exemplars are worth; does not make them a grading key.

likely_deductions.reasoning: The submissions break three written rules that this pack records independently: both finals run past the four-page body limit, one numbers its title page, and one power-curve pre-submission has no page numbers. On a report graded for technical writing, a deduction of that size is what those look like. Following the handout rather than the exemplar is therefore not only the safer rule, it is the specific way to close the gap the author describes.
likely_deductions.also_possible: An arithmetic or unit-conversion slip. A conversion error of exactly this class was found in this student's work for a different course, where a Fahrenheit reading was carried into a Kelvin calculation without conversion. Running results through `verify` catches that before submission; it is the one check a student cannot get by asking a model directly.
